articles.title: Charting the evolution of human–machine communication: a systematic review of 25 years of empirical research
articles.authors: Fanjue Liu, Xiaobei Chen, Kun Xu
articles.abstract: This study systematically examines trends and patterns in human–machine communication (HMC) research from 2000 to 2024. Based on a comprehensive screening of studies published in 28 communication and interdisciplinary journals and 2 foundational books, we analyzed 209 peer-reviewed articles based on their metadata, theoretical frameworks, research methods, technologies of interest, and research themes. The findings show steady growth in HMC scholarship following its formal recognition as a subfield with the establishment of the ICA Interest Group in 2019, continued reliance on social scientific research designs, and increasing interdisciplinary contributions. A BERTopic analysis identified 9 coherent research clusters, reflecting a gradual shift from robot-focused investigations toward a broader range of studies on virtual agents, chatbots, and generative AI. Overall, this review maps HMC’s intellectual trajectory and highlights key directions for future theoretical, methodological, and interdisciplinary development. It also discusses the increasingly ambiguous boundaries of HMC given the growing use of large language models and the convergent spaces between HMC and AI-mediated communication.

articles.title: (In)Visible politics: Influencers as brokers of the state on TikTok and Douyin
articles.abstract: Social media platforms are central to influencers’ pursuit of online visibility, yet little is known about how influencers strategically engage with the state across different political regimes to sustain that visibility. We examine how influencers on video-sharing platforms, many of whom originate in ostensibly non-political domains, navigate political crises as moments of intensified visibility, focusing on TikTok in Israel and Douyin in China. Drawing on a content analysis of 589 videos produced during Israel’s 2023 judicial reform and China’s 2020 COVID-19 crisis, we operationalize three visibility strategies: (1) state glamorization, (2) patriotic expression, and (3) out-group derogation as analytic lenses for examining how influencers broker the state within platform infrastructures. We show that influencers mobilize these strategies both proactively, by capitalizing on crisis-driven attention, and reactively, by aligning with dominant political narratives to avoid marginalization in saturated visibility environments. Across both cases, influencers operate as situational political brokers, translating state-linked discourse into platform-native vernaculars. We theorize political brokerage as a visibility practice emerging from transactional relations among influencers, platforms, and the state across democratic and authoritarian regimes, arguing that during moments of crisis, the state itself becomes a strategic visibility resource for influencers.

Social Media Use and Body Checking Behaviors: The Roles of Stress, Emotional Eating, and Self-Esteem
articles.authors: Aya Korkomaz, Sophia Jamal, Mariam Hakim, Nadine Zeeni
articles.abstract: Social media (SM) use has been associated with increased body image dissatisfaction and body checking behaviors. Repetitive exposure to idealized images and interaction with appearance-related content may be the cause of this relationship. The present study used a cross-sectional survey to examine the associations between body checking behaviors and SM use, emotional eating, perceived stress, and self-esteem among adults ( n = 423; aged 18–50 years, 71.9 percent female). Results showed that the number of online friends/followers, emotional eating, perceived stress, and general SM use significantly correlated with higher body checking scores. Conversely, self-esteem was negatively correlated with these scores. In multivariate regression analyses, perceived stress (B = 0.94, p < 0.001), emotional eating (B = 0.60, p < 0.001), general SM use (B = 0.18, p = 0.002), and lower educational level (B = −2.17, p = 0.011) independently predicted higher body checking scores, explaining 31.7 percent of the variance. These findings indicate that interventions focusing on media literacy and the management of stress and emotional eating may help mitigate the adverse effects of SM on body image and body-checking behaviors.

Comparing media systems in the digital age: A longitudinal research based on fuzzy set ideal type analysis
articles.abstract: Although research on media systems has empirically examined the three media system models proposed in Hallin and Mancini's landmark book Comparing Media Systems, longitudinal comparisons and ideal-type-oriented studies remain rare. These gaps limit scholars’ ability to observe how media systems evolve, particularly in the digital age, and to assess countries’ model membership and degrees of alignment. To fill these gaps, this study applied fuzzy set ideal type analysis to conduct a longitudinal comparison of the 18 countries included in Comparing Media Systems from 2010 to 2023. The findings reveal distinct variants of the classical models in the digital era, trace changes in countries’ ideal-type membership and degrees of alignment over time, and identify a representative case for each model.

articles.title: Technology-mediated communication among migrant families separated by borders: understanding the tensions of relational maintenance
articles.authors: Hyojin Lee, Jennifer A Kam, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Ricardo Delgado Solis, Amy Gonzales
articles.abstract: This study examined how highly under-resourced Latina/o/x/e families used technologically mediated communication to maintain their relationship when experiencing migration-based family separation. Drawing on relational maintenance literature, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 27 family triads, each including a father, mother, and child (children between 9 and 17 years old). The findings extend past research on relational maintenance by elucidating how structural barriers and culture contribute to tensions in relational maintenance and by providing within-family and between-family triangulated perspectives. Across families, three recurring relational maintenance strategies were consistently tensional: (a) sustaining routine contact, (b) prioritizing real-time interaction, and (c) practicing selective disclosure. The findings from within-family and between-family analyses showed how relational maintenance, which was primarily mediated by technology, became highly tensional under structural barriers and cultural norms and had unevenly distributed costs for family members.

articles.title: Negotiating algorithmic bias: discourses of techno-optimism and techno-hesitation in AI-mediated hiring
articles.abstract: Purpose Although artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated hiring is often viewed as a way to reduce human bias, it is commonly singled out as an example of algorithmic bias, which creates and amplifies inequalities. This article explores how the use of AI in hiring can be justified despite the existence of algorithmic bias. Design/methodology/approach Interviews and discourse analysis were conducted to examine how the use of AI in hiring can be justified despite algorithmic bias. Findings The interviewees expressed both techno-optimism and techno-hesitation when talking about AI in hiring. Techno-optimism emphasises that people make hiring processes biased and suggests that algorithmic bias can be addressed through a range of techniques such as fixing the data, fixing the human, “blinding” the algorithm and various processes of quality control and auditing algorithms. Rather than adopting techno-pessimism, the interviewees expressed techno-hesitation. Techno-hesitation refers to the acknowledgement of ethical concerns, followed by their reframing as managerial risks. Techno-optimism and techno-hesitation work together to justify the use of AI in hiring despite the risk of algorithmic bias. Originality/value Through theorising techno-hesitation, this article advances the literature by showing how ethical concerns can function as a resource for sustaining rather than disrupting AI adoption. The study contributes a novel analytical lens for understanding how legitimacy is discursively produced through the management, rather than the resolution, of ethical tensions surrounding AI-mediated hiring.

articles.title: Organizational autopoiesis and digital platforms in industry – exploring the conditions of self-referential decision-making
articles.abstract: Purpose The study investigates how firms can stay in control of their business and advance new business ventures when using digital platforms. Conceptually, it draws on social systems theory to address business ventures through self-referential decision-making in its course as a foundation of systemic autopoiesis and organizational programs informing such decisions. Design/methodology/approach To understand organizational programs and self-referential decision-making in platform use, problem-centered interviews are conducted with experts from industry. Content analysis reveals patterns of self-referential decision-making regarding the use of digital platforms from which different types of programs can be deduced. Findings When using digital platforms, self-referential decision-making splits up into a part that occurs on platforms in daily usage and off platforms when preparing and interpreting the use of platforms to conduct business. From these findings, conclusions can be drawn about different dimensions of organizational programming, concerning (1) frequency and level of aggregation in data sharing, (2) signaling in negotiations, presenting a firm, e.g. as bold, aggressive or reliable, stable, (3) reliance on personal ties and networks outside beyond the business activities address on the platform and (4) the direction of fit of platform data being either a descriptive approximation of business or a prescription for collaboration. Originality/value The study draws attention to autopoietic dynamics in business ecosystems that are essential for creative evolution driving economic development. It establishes a new approach to digital platforms through the lens of social systems theory with implications for theory development and the practice of platform design and operation.

“Human-like or cartoon-like?” The impact of virtual influencer style on consumer forgiveness propensity following service failures
articles.authors: Yizhi Liu, Ying Luo, Yu Liu, Meixing Li
articles.abstract: Purpose Virtual influencers have increasingly become a critical force in shaping consumer behavior. Accordingly, an in-depth examination of consumers’ response mechanisms following service failures by virtual influencers has emerged as an important research topic within the virtual influencer literature. Design/methodology/approach Using virtual influencer service failures as the research scenario, three experiments were conducted to examine consumers’ forgiveness propensity following service failures involving different types of virtual influencers. Findings The results of the three experiments show that, in service failure situations, compared with anthropomorphic virtual influencers, cartoon-like virtual influencers induce a higher level of consumer forgiveness propensity. This effect is mediated by responsibility attribution. Anthropomorphic virtual influencers are perceived as bearing greater responsibility because of their more salient human-like characteristics, which in turn, reduce consumers’ forgiveness propensity. The presence or absence of an algorithmic explanation affects consumers’ responsibility attribution for service failures, and uncanny perception negatively affects forgiveness propensity. Research limitations/implications This study focuses on recommendation failures and value-based failures and uses samples drawn from a specific cultural context. Future research could examine additional types of service failure, explore cross-cultural differences, and investigate dynamic service recovery processes over time. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for firms in selecting appropriate virtual influencer designs, managing algorithmic transparency, and developing effective service recovery strategies. Organizations should carefully balance anthropomorphic design and perceived uncanniness while tailoring communication strategies following service failures. Originality/value This study expands theoretical research on human–computer interaction and human-computer collaboration in the field of AI service marketing, while also providing practical insights for enterprises seeking to effectively optimize the remedial measures for virtual influencer service failures.

Trust Formation in AI Expert Systems
articles.abstract: Abstract: As artificial intelligence expert systems (AIES) are increasingly used in domains such as medicine, psychotherapy, law, finance, and education, it remains important to understand what shapes their perceived trustworthiness relative to human experts. A central limitation of prior research is that findings are often difficult to generalize across domains because domain and stakes are rarely varied together within the same design. We address this issue in a preregistered online vignette experiment in which UK participants ( N = 898) evaluated advice from an AIES and a human expert under low- and high-stakes conditions in one of five domains. Across all domains and both stake levels, human experts were perceived as more trustworthy than AIES, whereas AIES were perceived as riskier. For trustworthiness, between-domain effects were significant but small on average, mainly affecting the size of the human–AIES difference, which was largest in medicine and psychotherapy and smallest in education. For perceived risk, stakes played a larger role than domain, with high-stakes situations increasing perceived risk across domains. Importantly, trustworthiness and perceived risk did not change in parallel across conditions: Domain differences were comparatively small for trustworthiness, whereas stakes played a larger role in perceived risk. Overall, the findings suggest that cross-domain differences are smaller than often assumed once stakes are controlled, and that stakes matter more than domain for understanding perceived risk when people evaluate AIES advice.

articles.title: Person-Centered Support From Chatbots Versus Humans
articles.authors: Siyue Li, Runnan Wei, Shiyu Han, Mengwei Dang
articles.abstract: Abstract: This study aims to examine whether and how perceived identity of a support provider and message quality would affect perceived agency of the provider and support outcomes. A total of 196 college students in China participated in a laboratory experiment. Each participant was instructed to discuss a personal problem with either a chatbot or a human who would provide higher or lower person-centered support as preprogrammed. The results showed that perceived identity of a support provider and person-centeredness of support messages jointly affected participants’ perceptions of the provider agency, which in turn positively influenced participants’ emotional distress reduction, reappraisal, and perceived validation. The findings provide theoretical and pragmatic implications for the application of human–computer interaction in supportive communication.

articles.title: Extending Relational Turbulence Theory by Examining the Experiences of Latina/o/x/e Couples Facing Migration-Based Family Separation
articles.authors: Kyungin Kim, Jennifer A. Kam, Karla Vazquez, Ricardo Delgado Solis, Andrew C. High
articles.abstract: This study tested a portion of relational turbulence theory with 58 highly under-resourced Latina/o/x/e couples navigating migration-based family separation (i.e., where one partner migrated to the United States, while the other remained in a Latin American country, most often with their children). Couples completed pre- and post-conversation surveys and participated in an audio-recorded phone conversation discussing their experiences. Actor-partner interdependence mediation models (APIMeM) showed that pre-conversation self and partner uncertainty were positively related to post-conversation perceived partner disconnection (biased cognitive appraisals), which in turn was related to less openness about separation stress (communicative engagement) for partners in Latin America. Further, partner and relationship uncertainty of U.S.-based partners were indirectly related to less openness among partners in Latin America, highlighting the interdependent nature of partners’ relational experiences. Familismo only moderated one of the tested associations. Findings extend RTT’s applicability to this structurally and culturally distinct context and point to the urgency of providing stratified support for families facing systemically driven relational stress.

articles.title: Partner Sense of Purpose Predicts Personal and Relational Well-Being in Older Adult Couples
articles.authors: Jason A. Mitala, Brett K. Jakubiak, Yuxi Xie, Brooke C. Feeney
articles.abstract: One’s own sense of purpose is an important predictor of well-being in older adulthood. This research examines whether having a purposeful romantic partner predicts additional enhancements in one’s personal and relational well-being, beyond those explained by one’s own sense of purpose. Both members of older adult romantic couples reported their dispositional sense of purpose and their global well-being, then subsequently reported their daily well-being for seven days. We assessed whether own and partner dispositional sense of purpose predicted well-being (measured globally and measured momentarily in subsequent diary assessments). Beyond effects of one’s own sense of purpose on well-being, partner sense of purpose independently contributed to one’s greater life satisfaction, self-efficacy, relationship satisfaction, and commitment, as well as lower depression, stress, and loneliness (using both global and daily measures). Partner sense of purpose also independently predicted one’s experiences of lower global conflict and daily anxiety. Additional analyses indicated that it is the total purpose in the relationship (and not couples’ similarity in purpose) that predicts these positive outcomes. These findings imply that sense of purpose is a shared resource among older adult couples.

articles.title: “Thanks for the Clarification”: Denial of Responsibility Is Associated With Better Relationship Quality in Married Couples and Enhanced by Relationship Mindfulness
articles.authors: Daniel K. Smedley, Yunzhi Zheng, Jonathan G. Kimmes
articles.abstract: Although denying responsibility for relationship issues has been theorized as a maladaptive communication behavior, this construct lacks quantitative examination, and alternate theory suggests that denial of responsibility (DOR) may function as a form of direct cooperative communication that adaptively informs a partner’s evaluations of relationship quality, especially when done mindfully. Using a series of actor-partner moderation models (APIMoMs) with a sample of 115 married couples, we examined whether DOR was associated with partner perceptions of relationship quality (partner effects) and whether relationship mindfulness enhances the potential positive effects of DOR. Results showed that DOR was positively associated with better relationship quality, and this association was enhanced when paired with higher relationship mindfulness. These results suggest that DOR can be functional and cooperative, and that relationship mindfulness positively strengthens direct communication. Further replication of these findings may inform clinicians about when to nurture appropriate DOR (i.e., cooperative DOR) or reduce inappropriate DOR (i.e., defensive DOR), and the role of mindfulness in enhancing the potential benefits of DOR.

articles.title: Cynicism Explains the Link Between Subjective Social Class and Perceived Social Support Availability
articles.authors: Gregory T. H. Tan, Jacinth J. X. Tan
articles.abstract: Lower social class individuals tend to report less available support than higher social class individuals. The present research investigated whether lower subjective social class (SSC) individuals may perceive less available support because they are more cynical—or believe that people generally act in their personal interest. Study 1 examined the European Social Survey (Wave 6, N = 54,673) data that assessed individual reports of SSC, cynicism, and perceived social support availability across 29 countries. Path analyses revealed that lower SSC was associated with higher levels of cynicism, which in turn was associated with lower perceived available support. Study 2 sought to replicate the cynicism pathway in the lab and additionally examine if experimentally induced feelings of respect (versus disrespect) may reduce cynicism and increase perceived support availability among lower relative to higher SSC undergraduates ( N = 246). The overall cynicism pathway was replicated, although it was not mitigated by induced feelings of respect. In both studies, the alternative model where perceived support availability explains greater cynicism among lower SSC participants received less support. Our findings preliminarily highlight cynicism as a potential psychological barrier to seeking available social support among lower SSC individuals and the need to explore ways to mitigate cynical worldviews.

articles.title: Piloting the Integration of AI-Driven Detection Methods to Counter Disinformation in Organizational Processes
articles.abstract: With the rise of generative AI, the increasing threat of automatically generated uncivil content (including misinformation for information warfare up to cyber-bullying purposes) makes the protection of open online discourse even more pressing than before. In the implementation of measures for countering these threats, the different intervention objectives of stakeholders, their workflows, and IT support need to be considered. Stakeholders include online social network moderators, journalists, fact-checkers, social listeners, as well as authorities and organizations with safety- and security-related tasks. Given the sheer volume of online social network content, automated or community-based solutions are required to detect (automated) misinformation. However, detection solutions are predominantly message-focused and target end-users, leaving experts without systematic, large-scale perspectives on coordinated disinformation campaigns to guide countermeasures. To bridge this gap, we conduct an expert-centered study on the integration of detection methods proposed by the research community. Our contributions are threefold: (a) We adopt disinformation features from a previous study and draw connections to literature on detection methods; (b) semi-structured interviews yield vignettes that expose the spectrum of goals, constraints, tools, and decision-making processes employed by experts, informing requirements for method integration; (c) we design a demonstrator that showcases representative methods to uncover unexplored concepts, probe affordances and limitations in context, and evaluate conceptual fit during the interviews. Together, these steps bridge the gap between data- and AI-driven detection techniques from research and the practical needs of diverse stakeholders confronting targeted and large-scale disinformation.

articles.title: Free Smartphones? But Still Finding It Difficult to Find Place for Phones in Their Lives: Understanding Digital Interactions of Older Widow Women in Rural India
articles.abstract: This study is an exploration of the digital interactions of older widowed women living in rural India, who received free smartphones under a government scheme aimed at empowering marginalized women. Situated within the intersectionality framework, the research is an analysis of how the interplay of age, gender, widowhood, and rural residence shapes these women’s experiences with technology. Based on semistructured interviews with 16 widowed women aged 60–85 years, it was found in the study that the majority of the respondents are not using the smartphones themselves but have passed on the smartphones to younger female family members, citing utility to younger members and sociocultural norms. The study highlights the complex dynamics of digital inclusion in the Global South, where sociocultural factors lead to expectations that women conform to stereotypes about gender, age, and social status (being widowed) and, hence, significantly influence the adoption and use of technology. The study underscores the need for customized digital literacy initiatives that address both technical skills and the cultural stigmas surrounding technology use among older women living in rural areas. The study contributes to the discourse on the digital divide by focusing on a group that embodies several marginalities, offering insights for policy frameworks aimed at equitable digital empowerment.

articles.title: Rethinking platform vernaculars: Collective practices and power dynamics in platform environments
articles.abstract: In 2015, Gibbs et al. introduced the concept of platform vernaculars to describe how communicative genres emerge through interactions between platform affordances and user practices. Although widely adopted in media research, the concept has not been systematically refined in light of recent developments in affordance theory and platform studies. Drawing on an integrative literature review, this paper revisits platform vernaculars as plural, recognizable, repeatable, temporarily stabilized, and contested formations emerging through collective negotiations of affordances within platform environments. The paper further introduces four heuristic categories–intended vernaculars, dominant vernaculars, community vernaculars, and counter-public vernaculars–to discuss how communicative norms, genres, and modes of participation become normalized, marginalized, contested, or transformed across platforms. By rethinking platform vernaculars, the paper offers a systematic analytical framework for studying platform practices and norms. Furthermore, it positions vernaculars as a lens for analyzing platform power and user agency, opening avenues for future research.

articles.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Depressive Symptoms: The Mediating Role of Interpersonal Capitalization and Relationship Closeness
articles.authors: Sara Matovic, Nicolas Laporte, Linda Booij, Jean‐Philippe Gouin
articles.abstract: Prior research has mostly focused on the role of negative interpersonal processes in the association between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and depression. However, disruptions of positive interpersonal experiences may also be important. ACEs may reduce capitalization, the process of sharing good news with others, which contributes to experiencing closeness in relationships. This study examined whether capitalization and relationship closeness mediate the association between ACEs and depressive symptoms, over and above relationship stress, and whether these associations are amplified in a chronic stress context. Participants were 222 middle‐aged mothers experiencing varying degrees of chronic caregiving stress who reported on ACEs at baseline, and depressive symptoms as well as interpersonal processes at three time points over 30 months. Between‐person analyses of data aggregated across days and waves showed that higher ACEs were associated with lower capitalization, lower relationship closeness, and greater relationship stress. Relationship closeness and stress were associated with greater depressive symptoms, and a significant serial pathway emerged from ACEs to depressive symptoms via capitalization and relationship closeness. Caregiving stress amplified the association between ACEs and relationship stress. Findings suggest that ACEs may contribute to depressive symptoms in midlife through diminished positive interpersonal processes, independently of relationship stress and caregiving demands.

articles.title: Dyadic Validation of the Partner Emotion Work Scale: Evidence From Portuguese‐Speaking Couples
articles.authors: Francisca M. Moreira, Oscar Cervilla, Inês M. Tavares
articles.abstract: Emotion work—behaviors that enhance a partner's emotional well‐being—is central to couples' relational well‐being. The Partner Emotion Work (PEW) Scale is a well‐established measure of perceived emotion work, but no Portuguese version exists, and its validity has not been examined dyadically. This study translated, culturally adapted, and validated the PEW for use in Portugal in a sample of romantic couples, while also exploring its factor structure. Data from 155 dyads were used to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Portuguese PEW in both self‐referred and partner‐referred versions. Factor analyses supported a three‐factor model for each version: Emotional Support, Intimate Communication, and Companionship (Supportive and Affectionate). These dimensions represent complementary aspects of emotion work in couples; however, differences between self‐ and partner‐reports suggest that emotion work is perspective‐dependent. The Portuguese PEW showed strong psychometric properties, including content validity and expected associations with other variables. All subscales demonstrated good internal consistency. Overall, results support the Portuguese PEW as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing emotion work in romantic relationships from both self and partner perspectives.

articles.title: Social Media and the Smart City: A Systematic Review of City- and Citizen-Led Digital Spaces
articles.abstract: This systematic review examines how social media is conceptualized and studied within the context of smart cities, with a particular focus on the distinction between city-led and citizen-led digital spaces. Analyzing a sample of 50 peer-reviewed articles, the review identifies dominant techno-functionalist approaches that frame social media primarily as a data source for urban optimization, event detection, and service delivery. While some studies gesture toward participatory or socially embedded uses of social media, the majority lack engagement with specific urban contexts or active representations of cities and their citizens. The review highlights a significant gap in research on the actually existing smart city and the sociocultural dimensions of urban digital life. The findings underscore the need for future research to move beyond top-down, efficiency-driven narratives and to critically engage with emerging technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence, in both institutional and grassroots urban media practices. The article calls for a reimagining of smart cities and smart citizenship that centers participatory and socially grounded perspectives.

Media Use and Attitudes Toward Homosexuality: A Cross-National Analysis of the Moderating Roles of Polarization and Press Freedom
articles.abstract: The media can have an influential role in shaping citizens’ attitudes toward marginalized groups in society, such as homosexuals. Drawing from a cross-national survey sample from 43 countries ( N = 57,583), this study showed that traditional media use was related to negative attitudes toward homosexuals, while digital media use was positively related. The relationships were also contingent on levels of country-level societal political polarization and press freedom. Higher levels of polarization weaken the relationship between media use and attitudes toward homosexuals across media types. Under higher press freedom, traditional media are associated with higher justification of homosexuality and higher rejection of homosexual neighbors, while digital media use is associated with lower rejection of homosexual neighbors. These findings demonstrate that the relationship between media use and attitudes is to some extent contextual on a country’s political and media environment.

articles.title: The booming market for functional drinks in China: a multimodal critical discourse analysis of how packaging conveys notions of health
articles.abstract: In the context of the rising emphasis on health and healthy dieting in China, this article focuses on the booming market of functional drinks. The global market for such drinks has grown steadily and currently big international producers as well as local companies make huge investments in this field. The study concentrates on how functional drinks are promoted through their packaging design to appeal to Chinese consumers. Using the analytical tools of multimodal critical discourse analysis (MCDA), the analysis aims to reveal how notions of health and healthy ways of life are embedded in such mundane items. The data include two subcategories of functional drinks: vitamin/hydration drinks and health-improving drinks. Five of the most popular drinks were chosen from each category. The analysis shows that drinks are promoted as a form of ‘wonder drinks’ appealing to the aspirations of the rising Chinese middle class. Although the bottles have their obvious local design features, they are underpinned by the Western ideologies of nutritionism and the more self-centred morality of healthism, which contrasts with traditional Chinese values.

articles.title: Introduction to Special Issue on Food Packaging: Marketized health in the world’s cupboards
Wellness culture and Indigenous food imaginaries in South Africa: a multimodal critical discourse analysis of superfood marketing
articles.authors: Jiaqi Ye, Lame M Kenalemang-Palm, Fabio De Leonardis
articles.abstract: In South Africa, modernization and Western influence have produced remarkable dietary shifts, with rising consumption of meat, sugar and fat. These changes, coupled with growing public health concerns, have helped fuel a wellness culture in which superfoods are marketed as alternatives to highly processed food. This study uses multimodal critical discourse analysis (MCDA) to examine the digital marketing strategies of a South African food brand, Soaring Free Superfoods. This brand frames its products as sensually indulgent and scientifically grounded, promoting their nutritional value and health benefits, and attributing a distant Indigenous origin to their ingredients, which are presented as ‘natural’ and healthy. Moreover, the brand positions its products as symbols of moral virtue and health-consciousness, turning them into a symbolic capital distinguishing its consumers from the wider population. Overall, the marketing of Soaring Free products reflects the adaptation of healthy eating discourses prevalent in Western societies in a non-Western context.

articles.title: Milk packaging as a semiotic technology of the self
articles.abstract: At one level, food packaging would seem to perform an intermediary function by interceding between producers and consumers. In this sense, product packaging could be conceptualized as market actors who ‘construct’ or ‘add’ value by mediating how goods are perceived by consumers. Beyond matters of representation, however, food packaging can equally be understood as a means by which consumers gain and enact knowledge of themselves. In this way, food packaging does more than sell to a target market but also operates as a semiotic technology of the self. Using the example of ‘grass fed’ milk, a discourse–design approach is adopted, demonstrating how choices in packaging materials, textures and shapes, the colours applied, along with writing, typography and iconography not only qualify the selling features of a product but also contribute to consumers’ own self-understanding. Accordingly, it is argued that packaging should be understood as a medium through which consumers may come to experience themselves through the integration of the truth it bears regarding their own will and actions. In short, in using the grass-fed carton as a guide in their choice of milk product, consumers adopt truths about themselves as ethical subjects who demonstrate care for animals, family members and themselves.

articles.title: Selling international style healthy-branded foods in Malaysia: how the packaging design for ‘plant-based’ foods risks misleading/misdirecting consumers
articles.abstract: Scholars in food and nutrition studies have urged for more research on how global diets are entering into new territories around the world, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region, about which less is known. In particular, there is concern as diet-related disease tends to escalate after the arrival of supermarkets and ultra-processed foods. In this region, there has been growing government promotion of, and public interest in, healthy eating. However, food companies have also seen this as an opportunity to market healthy-branded foods which tend to be no better than highly processed foods in general. The danger is that these products can distract the public from actually eating a healthy, balanced diet, low in processed foods. In this article, looking at the context of Malaysia, where dietary shift and related illness have become particularly acute, the authors carry out a close analysis of an array of food packaging for a newly arrived product type: foods branded as ‘plant-based’. They seek to explore how such processed foods use this vague category to draw on a range of visual cues to present themselves as healthy options to the Malaysian public.

articles.title: Constructing Healthiness as a sense effect: A sociocultural semiotic analysis of Naturalness and Lightness on fruit drink packaging from Uruguay
articles.abstract: In order to expand research on how marketing communications influence consumers’ behaviour, this article adopts a sociocultural semiotic perspective focusing on text and social discourse to study fruit drink packages from Uruguay. Analysing the packages of fruit drinks usually referred to as ‘juices’ and fruit-flavoured waters, it demonstrates how producers strategically use visual and verbal semiotic resources expressing the values of Naturalness and Lightness, as these are effective in constructing a sense effect of Healthiness. Examining how visual resources such as figurative imagery of fruits and botanical elements, colours, fonts, shapes and the spatial disposition of design elements, together with verbal resources such as nutrient content claims (NCCs) are used, the analysis shows how an equivalence is established in this discursive genre between the values of Healthiness, Naturalness and Lightness, masking the industrial origin and processing of the products.

articles.title: ‘The cheese that tastes good and does good’: corporate social responsibility and national belonging in ICA’s Folke Cheese Initiative
articles.abstract: This article critically examines the Folke Cheese Initiative, a corporate social responsibility project launched by the Swedish supermarket retailer ICA in 2017 and linked to its hard cheese brand, Folke. Using an historical–archival approach to multimodal critical discourse analysis, the study traces the Initiative’s evolution across product development, launch and promotion, call to action and impact, analysing social media campaigns, promotional videos, packaging and websites. The analysis demonstrates how ICA constructs Folke as a symbol of national identity, embedding banal nationalist cues, familiar landscapes and rural imagery, while linking consumption to collective responsibility and social good. While the Initiative foregrounds community engagement, sustainability and national cohesion, it offers limited solutions to structural social and economic inequalities. Folke, thus, exemplifies how food packaging – and its associated promotional materials – can function as strategic instruments, aligning with Swedish social-democratic values while extending corporate influence over local communities. By presenting everyday consumption as a contribution to society, ICA positions itself as a socially responsible actor, even as the long-term efficacy of the Initiative remains uncertain. Overall, this case contributes new insights into the temporal evolution of corporate social responsibility (CSR) discourse, the multimodal construction of product-based social responsibility and the national specificity of sustainability practices in the Swedish food retail sector.

articles.title: Mexican food packaging in the era of new consumer protection regulations
articles.abstract: This article examines how food packaging communicates health and naturalness to Mexican consumers through design features, employing a historically-informed cultural framework. The research focuses on industrialized products made with dried corn flour, specifically tortillas and tostadas, analyzing how these packages utilize shape, color, images, and symbols to construct perceptions of health. The study investigates three brands: Sannísimo, produced by multinational foodprocessing firm Bimbo-Barcel, and two smaller brands, Señor Cactus and Sanopal, all marketed as ‘healthy’ product lines of Mexican staple foods. The analysis reveals how manufacturers strategically deploy national Mexican icons and notions of indigeneity to signify locality, authenticity, and sustainability, despite selling industrialized products. Food producers exploit environmental discourse to position their products as morally righteous choices while simultaneously linking them to wellness ideologies through intentional design strategies. This branding approach attempts to create what regulators term ‘health halos’, impressions that the foods are the best option in terms of nutrition and wellness. This research situates itself within the contemporary regulatory landscape where the Mexican state has implemented Front-of-Packaging Regulations, specifically NOM-051, to combat deceptive health marketing. These regulations establish that products displaying front-of-pack warning labels cannot include health claims on package fronts, representing a significant restriction aimed at protecting consumer interests. By analyzing how companies deal with these regulations, this study contributes to understanding the complex relationship between food marketing, public health policy, and consumer protection in Mexico. The findings illuminate tensions between corporate branding practices and state efforts to ensure transparent nutritional communication.

articles.title: Beyond choice: organic food packaging in French solidarity food initiatives
articles.abstract: This article examines the visual and material dimensions of food packaging in the PANIERS project – a French solidarity food initiative providing subsidized organic produce to 1,200 low-income families through partnerships with 27 organic farms. While extensive scholarship analyses how commercial organic brands use packaging to justify premium pricing and create social distinction, research on food banks and emergency food provision rarely examines the material containers and visual presentation of food itself. Through field-based semiotic analysis, this study investigates how PANIERS packaging – kraft paper bags, wooden crates, and information sheets – functions when removed from market competition. The findings reveal packaging operating beyond its conventional commercial function: it mediates relationships between farmers and recipients, communicates product qualities without market differentiation and circulates knowledge about agriculture and cooking. However, the minimalist aesthetic emerging from resource constraints aligns with visual codes that educated middle-class coordinators valorize as ethical consumption, but may communicate scarcity rather than choice to recipients experiencing material deprivation. This research advances Visual Communication scholarship by demonstrating how identical visual codes carry different meanings across organizational and economic contexts.

articles.title: Science or nature? A multimodal critical discourse analysis of breast milk substitutes packaging in China and the Netherlands
articles.abstract: This study explores multimodal discourse strategies adopted to promote breast milk substitutes (BMS) in two distinct socio-cultural contexts: China and the Netherlands. It scrutinizes how health-related values in these two countries are visually and verbally constructed by analyzing BMS product packaging. The approach used for this analysis is a combination of two methodological frameworks. First, the authors use a recently developed cohesion framework for multimodal packaging to organize data and identify different semiotic modes and expressive forms used in the various packages as well as their relationships in the meaning-making process. Second, they use a multimodal critical discourse analysis to examine how BMS companies navigate the political, economic and scientific landscapes of both nations to influence the discourse through the previously identified multimodal constructions. The findings show that nature-related themes on Dutch BMS packaging are rooted in local consumer perception of healthy food and align with the advocacy of these dietary guidelines. Chinese BMS packages, in contrast, place more emphasis on science-related themes, mainly because Chinese consumers’ understanding of healthy food leans more towards notions of safety, premium quality and guaranteed reliability. These findings reveal how cultural, social and economic contexts shape multimodal communication of health values through packaging, reflecting broader societal attitudes toward food and well-being.
